places.chef: owner · Yamashina-ku, Kyoto (near Keihan Yamashina / Yamashina Station) · Kawamura is a small tonkatsu specialist tucked into Yamashina, on the eastern edge of Kyoto. It began as a humble shop called Jukuton (熟豚, later とんかつ食堂熟豚) before being reborn under the current name 熟成豚 かわむら. The whole shop is built around one idea: aged pork. The pork is selected by farmers and then entrusted to a carcass-aging specialist in Kyoto's Fushimi district, where it is dry-aged for roughly three to five weeks so its aroma and flavor deepen before it ever reaches the fryer. The room is small and bright, almost cafe-like, with just a handful of counter and table seats, and it tends to fill the moment the doors open, even on weekdays. Word has spread well beyond Kyoto, and the little shop has been recognized in the Michelin Guide's Bib Gourmand. · Let the pork speak. places.chef: Kokichi Shimada (founder) · founder, second-generation chef-owner · Kyoto (Kiyamachi, then Gion) · Mimikou (味味香) began in 1969 as a Kiyamachi food stall opened by Kokichi Shimada, a former Japanese-restaurant (ryotei) owner, and grew into a Kyoto curry-udon institution. The shop relocated to its present spot in Gion near Yasaka Shrine in June 2010, and its curry udon was recognized in 2015 by Japan's Cool Japan 'The Wonder 500' selection. · Honoring the founder's original recipe while refining it: the second-generation owner, who trained in French cuisine, spent years perfecting the dashi (kombu and dried bonito for the regular broth, and a fish-free version for vegetarian diners) and the balance of spices, treating the curry udon as Kyoto 'soul food.' · Kyoto-style curry udon: chewy udon in a deeply flavored ankake (thick) curry broth. places.chef: Dai Okonogi (小此木 大) · owner, chef · From Aichi Prefecture, Japan; based in Kyoto · TADKA's owner-chef, Dai Okonogi (小此木 大), originally from Aichi Prefecture, trained at Mughal, a long-established Indian restaurant in Kyoto, before opening TADKA1 in 2012 as a street-stall-style South Indian lunch spot on Oshikoji-dori. places.chef: Shojin ryori restaurant, Sagano/Arashiyama branch of the Izusen company · Kyoto, Japan · Izusen (泉仙) is a long-established Kyoto purveyor of shojin ryori — Buddhist Zen temple vegetarian cuisine — with roots in the city's monastic catering tradition. The Sagano branch sits in the historic Sagano/Toriimoto district near Arashiyama and serves the same teppatsu (iron-bowl) shojin style for which the company is known across its Kyoto locations (including its temple branch at Daiji-in within the Daitoku-ji complex). · Rooted in Zen Buddhist practice, the food is entirely plant-based, seasonal, and prepared with the shojin ethos of simplicity, gratitude, and non-killing — eating in harmony with nature and the temple calendar. · Teppatsu shojin ryori — a course meal served in a set of nested red-lacquer (朱塗り) bowls (typically seven, graded large to small) modeled on the teppatsu, the iron alms bowl monks historically carried to receive offerings. Signature items include sticky, nutty sesame tofu (goma-dofu), tofu fritters, vegetable tempura (shojin-age) such as shiitake, and simmered and vinegared/dressed seasonal vegetables, finished with matcha and a Japanese sweet.
places.gfd: Not gluten-friendly. Wheat-based soy sauce and fu (wheat gluten) are essential, core ingredients in Izusen's cooking and cannot be modified, per InsideKyoto. Tempura batter and other course components also typically contain wheat flour. A celiac or strictly gluten-free diner should not rely on this restaurant; there is no dedicated GF menu or accommodation noted.
places.vgd: Izusen serves shojin ryori (Buddhist temple vegetarian cuisine) that is entirely plant-based, with no meat or fish. places.chef: ramen shop, tsukemen specialist · Kyoto · 麺や高倉二条 is the head shop of a small, tightly run Kyoto ramen family that also includes the Sugari shops and a couple of sibling counters. places.chef: owner-chef · 頑固麺 sits in the Fukakusa stretch of Fushimi, one of Kyoto's most competitive ramen districts, a short walk from Fujinomori Station. The owner trained at a well-regarded Fushimi-Momoyama ramen shop before striking out on his own, and the place has become a lunchtime fixture that draws lines even on weekdays despite being open only midday. · The shop's name plays on 頑固 ('stubborn'); the kitchen leans into a single-minded pursuit of a fully-realized, concentrated bowl. A house condiment nicknamed the 'Ganko sauce' is offered as a flavor intensifier so diners can dial the broth up to one of the densest in Kyoto. · The signature is a thick chicken-pork-bone bowl (とりとんこつ): chicken slowly simmered down to a rich, almost paste-thick consistency, with pork umami arriving on the finish, yet kept clean and approachable rather than heavy. It is paired with snappy medium-thin wavy noodles from Kyoto noodle maker Menya Teigaku (麺屋棣鄂), topped with large rare chashu, menma, onion and a hit of mayu (burnt-garlic oil). Variations include 煮干しとりとんこつ (with dried sardine), 濃厚醤油とりとんこつ (rich soy), 鶏中華そば, and a back-fat 背脂 mazesoba.

places.chef: Tatsuo Uemura (上村) · owner, chef · Kyoto, Japan (Shimogyo-ku, near Shijo-Karasuma) · Born in 1954, Uemura worked for a fish company before moving to Kansai and running several restaurants. He briefly closed early on to refine his recipe after realizing Kyoto's hot, humid summer (the shop opened in August) shifted customers' taste away from the cold-northern, heavily-salted style he had trained in. · Uemura rejects a profit-first approach, saying he doesn't think of ramen as a money-making tool and prioritizing quality over margin. He wants guests to taste attentively — phones and reading are discouraged at the counter, and children under elementary-school age are not admitted because he wants diners with a developed enough palate to appreciate the subtlety of the broth. · The 天然塩らーめん (natural-salt ramen) is the signature bowl — a clear, golden broth built on a rare cooking technique. places.chef: Sasaki Koji · owner-chef, family-run kitchen · Kyoto (Gion lineage, Beijing-style Chinese cuisine) · Seikatei opened in 1982 in the quiet temple district near Ginkaku-ji. Its roots run back to 盛京亭 (Seikyotei), a Beijing-style restaurant founded in 1951 in the heart of Gion's hanamachi (geisha district). Seikatei keeps that restraint — light white-pressed soybean oil (shirashime-yu), local Matsui-brewery sake instead of cooking wine, and clean, delicate flavors over punch. · Goma-gyoza (sesame dumplings): roasted sesame is kneaded right into the wrapper, with a filling of only cabbage, Chinese chives, pork and sake, then pan-fried in a heavy cast iron pan until the surface turns crisp. It began as an off-menu request from a regular and became the house signature.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto — Gion / Higashiyama · にぼ魂 opened on August 8, 2025 in the heart of Gion, just north of Gion-Shijo Station off Nawate-dori, taking over a space that had until then housed a kasu-udon shop (かすうどん). It was conceived from the start as a deep-night niboshi-ramen stop — a bowl to land in after an evening out in Gion's bars and teahouses, when most kitchens have long closed, running from around 8pm into the early-morning hours. · Lean into the niboshi rather than tame it — a punchy, sea-forward bowl built for the late-night palate, served bright and clean in a small room. places.chef: second shop / sister brand of Fukakusa Seimen Shokudo · Kyoto (Fushimi/Fukakusa lineage) · Menya Ikku opened on April 10, 2018, about a one-minute walk from JR Nishioji Station as the second shop and sister brand of Fukakusa Seimen Shokudo, a well-regarded ramen maker based in Fushimi Ward. Its debut was marked by a storefront crowded with congratulatory flowers. The space is deliberately stylish and modern, closer to a cafe-bar than a traditional ramen counter, with an upper floor above the ground-floor dining room. · Coax maximum depth from quality regional chicken through long, careful simmering, presented in a clean, design-forward setting rather than a rough-and-ready ramen joint. · A rich chicken paitan (tori-paitan) ramen. places.chef: owner-proprietor (female proprietor, descendant of the geisha Takeka) · Gion, Kyoto · Takeka opened in 1966 at the foot of Gion Shinbashi, beside the Shirakawa stream, and has spent close to six decades cooking for the geiko and maiko, teahouse patrons, and locals of the district. places.chef: Hamamura Hozo (founder, 濱村保三); third-generation Hamamura Yoshiyuki (濱村吉行) · founder, third-generation owner-operator · Kyoto, Japan · Hamamura was founded in 1924 (Taisho 13) and is widely credited as the birthplace of Kyoto Chinese (kyo-chuka). What began as a humble noodle-and-Chinese shop grew into one of the city's defining culinary lineages, now run by the founder's grandson, the third-generation Hamamura Yoshiyuki. The Fuchomae branch sits across from the Kyoto Prefectural Office and moved to this Marutamachi spot from Kawaramachi around 2014. · Kyoto Chinese holds back the garlic and heavy oil of mainland Chinese cooking, leaning instead on chicken-bone and kombu dashi for a clean, restrained flavor. The style is said to have grown out of Kyoto's geisha districts, where strong-smelling foods were discouraged. · The signature dish is karashi-soba: noodles bound in a glossy ankake sauce sharpened with vinegar-loosened Japanese mustard, described as spicy yet paradoxically light and refined. Their straightforward chuka-soba is the other anchor of the menu.
places.gfd: No gluten-free options. The signature noodle dishes — 中華そば and the famous からしそば — use wheat noodles, and the からしそば is finished with a wheat-thickened ankake sauce and mustard. places.chef: Kirameki group branch · Kyoto (Kirameki group, flagship in Marutamachi) · A Kami-Katsura neighborhood ramen shop in Kyoto's Nishikyo Ward, this is one branch of the fast-growing Kirameki group, which began with its flagship Kirameki no Tori in Marutamachi and has spread across Kyoto and into Osaka. The signature bowl is Komugi no Chikara ('the power of wheat'), a Jiro-style thick-noodle mazesoba piled with bean sprouts, menma, and big chunks of tender pork and back fat. places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto (Takano / Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku) · Ramen Viska opened on July 14, 2023, in a quiet residential pocket behind Takano Post Office, on the fringe of Ichijoji's famously crowded ramen battleground. It is a true one-person shop: the owner cooks, serves, and chats single-handedly. The space is a renovated former snack bar with a glossy high bar-style counter of about five seats, and the owner greets guests in a suit and tie rather than the usual ramen-cook garb. There is no noren curtain out front. · A minimalist, single-minded devotion to tonkotsu done well — quality broth over a broad menu, served personally and explained in detail to anyone curious. · Super-rich kotteri tonkotsu: a pork-bone broth simmered until thick enough that, as locals joke, the spoon could stand up in it, yet it stays mild and clean on the palate with no porky funk, drinking almost like a potage. The lineup is deliberately spare — kotteri (rich), assari (a remarkably clear, transparent tonkotsu, finished with yuzu zest), a Bisuro (ビス郎) bowl, and tsukemen — paired with medium-straight noodles and well-seasoned roast-pork chashu. The focus is entirely the bowl.
places.gfd: This is a wheat-noodle tonkotsu shop with no gluten-free offering. places.chef: owner · Kyoto · Kyogame occupies a restored Kyoto machiya townhouse along Imadegawa-dori, a short walk from Demachiyanagi. The owner, known affectionately as Kame-san, runs it less like a polished restaurant and more like a friend's home — courtyard garden, tatami rooms where you can stretch your legs, and the unhurried feel of an old popular izakaya. · Generous, unfussy, and deliberately affordable — the lunch bowls are priced so that students and regulars can come often, in a room meant to feel like dropping by someone's house rather than dining out. · The house centerpiece is a hearty garlic motsunabe: select beef offal in a quality chicken-bone broth, offered in white-miso, soy, or salt versions, alongside other izakaya sides. At lunch the kitchen turns to ramen — the signature being a cabbage-piled hormone (offal) ramen, alongside a light clam (asari) salt bowl and, in summer, a cold duck-and-vegetable bowl, all served with a generous 1.5 portions of noodles.
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The lunch bowls are standard wheat ramen noodles, and the kitchen is built around motsunabe with chicken/garlic broths and soy-based seasonings — no gluten-free noodles, dedicated handling, or allergen accommodation is advertised. Cross-contamination with wheat is effectively guaranteed in a shared ramen and hotpot kitchen.

places.chef: owner · Kyoto (originally Uzumasa / west Kyoto) · Sugichiyo is the revival of a legendary Kyoto ramen shop. The original opened in 1999 in the Uzumasa area of western Kyoto and drew daily lines for roughly a decade before it closed at the end of 2009 — reportedly because the crowds it attracted had become difficult to sustain. After about twelve years dormant, the name returned in June 2021 in a renovated spot down a Takase River alley just west of Shijo-Kawaramachi, in the heart of central Kyoto's nightlife district. The current team is said to have inherited the complete original recipe directly from the founder. · Faithfully carry forward a beloved recipe rather than reinvent it — a nostalgic, unpretentious bowl served with quiet, courteous hospitality instead of the high-intensity style of many modern ramen shops. · Chashu ramen — the bowl that built the shop's reputation. The pork-bone soy-sauce broth carries the deep richness of Kyoto-style ramen with a thin veil of back fat on top, yet drinks lighter and cleaner than its color suggests; the soy tare is comparatively restrained, letting the broth's umami lead. places.chef: owner-operator · Matsugasaki, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto · 麺屋 しな埜 began life in February 2020 as TETSUpan Style+ しな埜, a yakisoba specialty shop, before reinventing itself as a ramen-focused restaurant in March 2021 with chicken paitan as its new signature. A further full renovation in September 2024 refreshed the menu and the space. It sits, almost unexpectedly, in a quiet residential pocket of Matsugasaki near the ward office, drawing queues to a converted white single-family house with sunlit counter seating and a breezy balcony area. · Rather than the heavier bowls Kyoto is often known for, the shop leans on technique and restraint, using the whipped-foam broth and carefully drawn dashi to keep flavors smooth and the finish clean. · The house bowl is the 泡白湯 (awa paitan): a broth simmered from whole chicken and chicken bones, then whipped into a creamy, mousse-like foam and finished with a Japanese-style soy tare for a surprisingly clean, light aftertaste. The kitchen also offers a chicken paitan, a fish-soy (gyokai-shoyu) ramen built on a low-temperature dashi of three fish flakes, kombu and dried shiitake with chicken oil, and a rich fish-pork tsukemen.
places.gfd: Not gluten-free and not suitable for celiacs. This is a classic ramen shop: wheat noodles served in a chicken paitan or fish-soy broth finished with soy-sauce-based tare (Japanese soy sauce / white soy sauce, both wheat-containing). Tsukemen (dipping noodles) is also wheat. No gluten-free menu, no documented allergen accommodation.
places.vgd: No vegan options. The signature bowls are built on a chicken-based broth (whole chicken and chicken bones), with chashu, flavored egg, and other animal toppings; the fish-soy ramen uses fish-flake dashi. Nothing on the menu is plant-based.

places.chef: Mr.京都アッキー (Mr. Kyoto Akky) · owner, chef, food YouTuber · Kyoto, Japan · Akky is a Kyoto native who became well known across the city's ramen scene as a food creator, running the YouTube channel 'Mr.京都アッキーのぶらり飲食店巡り' along with TikTok, Instagram and X, where he tirelessly reviewed Kyoto ramen shops. Before opening this place he spent about two years running a ramen shop on borrowed premises in Fushimi, learning the craft hands-on, before launching his own standalone shop in Shimogamo in August 2025. · Akky builds everything on a 100% pork broth simmered carefully from early morning, drawing out the depth of pork bone and pork meat while keeping the finish clean rather than heavy. He describes the goal as a soup that is rich yet sharp ('コクがありながらもキレのある'), an everyday bowl that people of all ages can enjoy. · His signature is the 'Triple GO' back-fat black chuka soba (トリプルGO 背脂ブラック中華そば) - a dark soy-and-back-fat bowl in the classic Kyoto 'black' style - alongside a back-fat tonkotsu-shoyu chuka soba.

places.chef: owner-chef · 京都市下京区 七条大宮・梅小路 · A small, time-worn ramen counter tucked into the Shichijo-Omiya block near Umekoji Park and Umekoji-Kyoto-Nishi Station. It belongs to Kyoto's beloved 'Akira-kei' (旭系) lineage — the nostalgic Kyoto soy-sauce ramen tradition associated with the famous Daiichi-Asahi. The owner is said to have trained at a shop called Taiki before opening his own counter, and the place has the lived-in, slightly aged storefront of a long-standing local fixture. · A taciturn owner with a quiet, single-minded devotion to ramen — no frills, no trend-chasing, just an honest bowl in the old Kyoto idiom. Regulars describe the flavor as deeply nostalgic, evoking long-gone neighborhood shops. · Kyoto-style shoyu ramen — a clear, pork-forward broth where the pig's umami and richness are balanced against a restrained soy edge, served over soft medium-thick straight noodles that soak up the broth, finished with loin chashu, a generous pile of scallions and bean sprouts. A miso version and a notably good spicy miso are also offered.

Not suitable for celiacs. The only other listed item is gyoza (wheat wrappers). Assume cross-contamination throughout a single shared kitchen.

places.chef: owner-operator, successor (founder's younger brother carrying on the recipe) · Kyoto · Shinshintei is widely credited as the birthplace of Kyoto-style white miso ramen. The lineage began as a humble food stall around 1960 and grew into a brick-and-mortar shop opened in 1972 in the Fushacho area of central Kyoto. Over nearly four decades it built a devoted following before the original first-generation owner retired and closed that location in 2009 due to age. Rather than let the recipe disappear, the founder's younger brother inherited the name and the noren and reopened the shop in the Ichijoji district, where it carries the tradition forward today as a lunch-only neighborhood institution. · Keep the original white-miso recipe alive and unchanged - a mellow, comforting, deeply flavored bowl made the same way it has been for decades, served simply at lunch. · The signature bowl is white miso ramen (白味噌ラーメン) - a gentle, mellow, slightly sweet white-miso broth that is distinct from the heartier Sapporo style. It pairs a concentrated dashi with a light white miso (淡めの白味噌), is piled with plenty of vegetables, and is served with straight Kyoto-style noodles that meet the smooth broth.

places.chef: tonkotsu ramen specialist · Ichijoji, Sakyo Ward, Kyoto · Kyomenya opened on December 12, 2016 along Ichijoji's famously competitive ramen street in Kyoto's Sakyo Ward, near the well-known Ramen Yokozuna. It carved out its niche by going against the grain: while Ichijoji leans toward lighter chicken-based broths, Kyomenya planted its flag on unapologetically heavy, ultra-rich tonkotsu. · The aim is a broth that is intensely rich and creamy — dorodoro thick — yet kept smooth and balanced rather than merely heavy (濃厚ですがくどさはありません), with the pork bone simmered long and combined with seafood stock for depth. · The flagship bowl is the Kyo-no Tonkotsu (驚濃とんこつ) — a viscous, cream-thick pork-bone broth rounded out with seafood dashi, using roughly three times the pork bone of an ordinary tonkotsu ramen (通常の豚骨ラーメンの約3倍). places.chef: owner-chef · Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto · 本気つけ麺山下 opened on May 25, 2026 in the heart of Ichijoji, the neighborhood widely regarded as Kyoto's most fiercely competitive ramen district. It took over the space of the well-loved shop "Tsurukame Ichijoji," which closed at the end of March 2026, refreshing the storefront into a clean, bright counter room of eight seats. The proprietor is understood to have trained at a well-known ramen establishment before striking out on his own here. · The shop keeps its focus deliberately narrow, offering only its two tsukemen and letting the noodles and dip do the talking, with a stated wish to become a place loved by many. · A two-bowl tsukemen specialist. The second pillar, 胡麻豆乳担々つけ麺, folds rich roasted sesame and creamy soy milk into a tantan dip crowned with meat-miso for a richness-meets-balance bowl.

places.chef: Noriko Fujita (藤田典子) · owner, chef · Kyoto · The owner spent years as a hospital nurse, earning her nursing credentials while raising her family and returning to study around age 38 after her children grew more independent. Working grueling night shifts, she found that a bowl of ramen eaten after coming off a night shift restored both her stamina and her spirit. That comfort became a calling: at 53 she set out to open her own shop. · She refused to cut corners with wholesale noodles, investing in a professional noodle machine (from Daikoku Manufacturing, around 2.7 million yen) so she could make her own noodles in-house, because she wants customers to taste the difference of truly handmade noodles. Sitting near the universities, she also wants to send students and young people off well-fed and happy, an extension of her caretaking instincts from nursing into feeding her community. · Jiro-style ramen with generous pork and vegetable toppings; the signature is the 小豚ラーメン (kobuta / small-pork ramen). Bowls are customized at order time by noodle quantity and the classic Jiro toppings of garlic, extra vegetables, and oil.

places.cu: Chicken-tonkotsu paitan ramen

rm.bowl: 肉白湯そば (Niku Paitan Soba) — a thick, emulsified chicken-and-pork-bone white broth finished with a special chicken paste you stir in to deepen the richness, topped with a pepper accent.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Menya Shourin opened on February 10, 2020 in the leafy Kamigamo district of Kyoto's Kita Ward, just north of Kamigamo Shrine near Kyoto Sangyo University. The owner trained at the well-known Kyoto ramen group Kirameki no Tori (キラメキノトリ) before striking out on his own.
places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto (Kamigamo / Kita Ward) · Menya Shourin opened on February 10, 2020 in the leafy Kamigamo district of Kyoto's Kita Ward, just north of Kamigamo Shrine near Kyoto Sangyo University. The owner trained at the well-known Kyoto ramen group Kirameki no Tori (キラメキノトリ) before striking out on his own. · Careful broth-making aimed at a rich umami with no off-flavors (雑味のない、まろやかな味), served in a clean, café-like space welcoming to students, families and locals. · The signature bowl is the niku-paitan soba (肉白湯そば) — an emulsified chicken-and-pork-bone (鶏豚骨) white broth that is full-bodied yet clean and mellow, finished with coarse black pepper. A special chicken paste is meant to be stirred in partway through to deepen the flavor. Straight, medium-thin noodles come from the respected Teigaku (棣鄂) noodle maker. The menu rounds out with a tori-chuka soba and a spicy kara-niku mazesoba.
places.gfd: A chicken-pork paitan ramen shop with no gluten-free offerings. Noodles are wheat (sourced from the well-known Teigaku/棣鄂 noodle maker), broth and tare are standard, and mazesoba/fried-chicken sides involve wheat. Not suitable for celiacs; no GF accommodation noted on any source.
places.vgd: Every bowl is built on an animal base — a rich emulsified chicken-and-pork-bone (鶏豚骨) white broth, with meat toppings and a chicken paste stirred in mid-meal. There are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options; sides include fried chicken and rice. No plant-based menu noted.

Tucked into a quiet residential block south of Misonobashi near Kamigamo, it later changed its business format to a ramen shop while keeping the same name and its sho
places.chef: owner-chef · Garamon began life not as a ramen shop but as a charcoal-grill yakitori izakaya called 炭焼賀ら茂ん (Sumiyaki Garamon). Tucked into a quiet residential block south of Misonobashi near Kamigamo, it later changed its business format to a ramen shop while keeping the same name and its shoes-off, lived-in izakaya feel. · An owner-run, single-counter shop designed so one person can comfortably walk in and eat well for cheap; quiet, residential, no-frills, with the kitchen's attention going into the dashi-forward broth and the seared pork rather than spectacle. · Two bowls anchor the menu, both at the same modest price: a lighter 中華そば (chuka soba) and a richer 背脂醤油 (sebabura shoyu) with back-fat and added oil. The broth blends pork bone, chicken carcass, kombu and seafood, leaning unusually far toward a Japanese dashi character so that it edges toward udon/soba territory while keeping ramen body and sweetness. The signature topping is a thick slice of aburi (seared) chashu, individually torched and brushed with glaze for aroma.
places.gfd: This is a traditional chuka soba / seb-abura shoyu ramen shop. The bowls are built on wheat noodles and a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare, which in Japan is almost always brewed with wheat, over a pork-bone, chicken, kombu and seafood broth. No gluten-free noodles, tare, or accommodations are mentioned in any source, and there is no indication the kitchen handles celiac-level allergen requests. Not suitable for anyone needing to avoid gluten.
places.vgd: The signature bowls are built on a pork-bone, chicken and seafood (fish/kombu) broth and are topped with seared chashu pork. There are no vegan or vegetarian ramen options described anywhere; the menu centers on animal-based broths and meat toppings.
places.hours: Mon, Tue, Thu, Fri, Sat 11:30-18:00; Sun & holidays 11:30-15:00; closed Wednesday. Hours can change month to month; the owner posts a monthly calendar on X (Twitter).

places.chef: owner · 京都市北区 衣笠 · This Kinugasa noodle shop opened in October 2025 in the very space that was long home to a beloved local Chinese restaurant known for its tantanmen. The earlier shop had built a quiet reputation around the neighborhood for its dan dan noodles; when the room was reborn as a dedicated tantanmen specialist, the recipe was carried forward and refined, and the dining room was brightened into something that feels a touch more like a polished Chinese restaurant than a quick noodle stop. · Rather than chasing the fiery, mala-heavy style, the shop leans into a mild, comforting take on tantanmen and puts the heat in the diner's hands: the tables are set with chili oil, garlic chili oil, chili powder, Sichuan pepper, black pepper, salt, soy sauce and vinegar so each guest can dial the bowl up to taste. · The house bowl is a deliberately non-spicy, Kyoto-style tantanmen, offered both with broth (汁あり) and brothless (汁なし). It is a compact, clean, counter-only shop run as essentially a one-person operation, where guests buy a ticket from the machine before orderi
places.chef: owner-operator · Ichijoji, Sakyo Ward, Kyoto · Arajin opened on September 10, 2014, on a corner of the Ichijoji intersection — one of Kyoto's most intensely competitive ramen districts. It is a compact, clean, counter-only shop (about 12 seats) run as essentially a one-person operation, where guests buy a ticket from the machine before ordering. · The cooking leans on careful craftsmanship — a broth made rich without becoming heavy, and medium-thick, hand-kneaded-style noodles specially ordered from an established noodle maker for good chew and slurp. The result is described as crave-worthy and habit-forming. · The signature bowl is the rich miso tonkotsu ramen (濃厚味噌豚骨ラーメン): a creamy, full-bodied pork-bone broth carrying the depth and aroma of miso, finished with back fat, and rounded out with green onion, thin-sliced chashu, half a seasoned egg, nori, menma, and sesame. A shoyu tonkotsu version is the other pillar of the menu.
places.gfd: Ramen here is wheat noodles (medium-thick noodles from a noodle factory) in pork-bone broth flavored with miso or soy tare, which typically contains wheat. No gluten-free options and no indication of allergy accommodation; not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: A pork-bone (tonkotsu) ramen specialist; the signature bowls are built on rich pork broth with chashu, egg, and back fat. There is no vegan or vegetable-based ramen offering.
places.hours: 11:30–14:30 (lunch), 18:00–21:00 (dinner); closed Tuesdays. Note: some sources list the dinner close as 22:00.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A neighborhood ramen counter tucked near the Hyakumanben crossing west of Kyoto University, Takumi has been feeding locals and students for close to two decades. It is the kind of unpretentious machi-chuka spot you slip into for a satisfying, affordable bowl, including late at ni
places.chef: owner · A neighborhood ramen counter tucked near the Hyakumanben crossing west of Kyoto University, Takumi has been feeding locals and students for close to two decades. It is the kind of unpretentious machi-chuka spot you slip into for a satisfying, affordable bowl, including late at night. · Comfort over flash: carefully drawn-out broth, an almost extravagant amount of negi, and a friendly counter feel that has kept regulars coming back for years. · The signature is the Takumi Chashu-men: a bowl piled with thin slices of chashu pork arranged like overflowing flower petals, set over a long-simmered pork-bone (tonkotsu) soy-sauce broth that is at once viscous and mellow, without any heavy or off-putting edge. A generous heap of Kujo-style green onion crowns the bowl, cutting the richness so it eats clean and bright. A lighter, clear shoyu chuka-soba is also offered for those who want something more delicate.
places.gfd: This is a traditional chuka-soba (ramen) shop: wheat noodles in a pork-bone/soy-sauce broth, with a wheat-based shoyu tare. There is no indication of any gluten-free noodle, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. A celiac or strictly gluten-free diner cannot safely eat the ramen here, and nothing on the menu (ramen, tsukemen, gyoza) is gluten-free. Treat as not suitable.
places.vgd: The house broth is built on long-simmered pork bones (tonkotsu) and the bowls are crowned with chashu pork, so the core offering is not vegan or vegetarian. There is no listed plant-based broth or noodle option. A vegan diner has no suitable bowl here.

That tradition traces back to Takahashi Kakitsu (高華吉), the chef
places.chef: 相場哲夫 (Tetsuo Aiba) · Kyoto-Chinese restaurant, からしそば specialist, 鳳舞 (Houmai) lineage · Kyoto (Kamigyō-ku, Imadegawa) · 鳳舞楼 carries forward one of Kyoto's most beloved culinary lineages: that of 鳳舞 (Houmai), the legendary Kyoto-Chinese restaurant opened by chef 高華吉 (Kō Kakichi) in 1967 and closed in 2009, within whose walls generations of Kyoto families held their celebrations. Kyoto-style Chinese itself traces back further, to 支那料理ハマムラ (Hamamura), the city's first Chinese restaurant, opened in Gion in 1924 by 濱村保三; it was there that Kō Kakichi honed the approach of lightening Chinese dishes with Japanese dashi to suit Kyoto's refined, geisha-district palate before founding his own 鳳舞. After the original Houmai shuttered, its apprentices fanned out across the city to keep the style alive, a network locals call the '鳳舞系' (Houmai lineage). 鳳舞楼 is part of that lineage, now settled in a bright, modern room steps from Imadegawa Station with views toward the Kyoto Imperial Palace and Doshisha University. · あっさり上品な京中華 — light, refined Kyoto Chinese. places.chef: 芥川 (Akutagawa) · owner, founder · Yokohama iekei lineage via Ramen Musashi-ya (ラーメン武蔵屋) · Founder Akutagawa and his colleague Hirayama (who became a later shop owner) met working at Ramen Musashi-ya, the parent shop in the iekei (家系) tradition. The two set out to bring real Yokohama-style iekei ramen to Kyoto, scouring the city by bicycle until they found the spot on Imadegawa, just east of the Hyakumanben intersection by Kyoto University's main gate, opening on September 8, 2018. · Keep it honest and accessible: Akutagawa held the bowl to the parent shop's price point even as he sourced ingredients carefully, absorbing higher costs through tight management so students and locals could afford a serious bowl. He framed the work around how much he could give back to customers. · The standard bowl (並ラーメン) of rich pork-and-chicken-bone tonkotsu-shoyu broth, built iekei-style by continuously replenishing the stock (継ぎ足し). It comes with thick noodles, thick-cut pork loin chashu, spinach, and sheets of nori, with free bean-sprout namul and refillable rice on the side. Diners are asked their preferences for noodle firmness, broth strength, and back fat.
places.gfd: This is a Yokohama iekei (家系) ramen shop. No gluten-free noodles, broth, or accommodations are mentioned anywhere. Not safe for celiac diners.
places.vgd: A tonkotsu (pork-bone) and chicken-bone broth shop. The signature bowl includes pork chashu, and the broth itself is animal-based, so it is not suitable for vegans or vegetarians. The free rice and bean-sprout sides are not a meaningful vegan path here. No plant-based ramen offered.

It was founded by the previous master and has since passed to the n
places.chef: second-generation owner · Yamashina, Kyoto · Yonakiya is one of the old guard of Kyoto ramen, a shop that has stood along the Nara-kaido road in the Otsuka district of Yamashina for decades and is treated as one of the originals of the city's ramen lineage. It was founded by the previous master and has since passed to the next generation, who carries on the same single-bowl tradition. · A one-bowl shop in the truest sense: it does essentially one thing, the old Kyoto chuka soba, and has done it the same way long enough that decades of consistency on a single corner are taken as proof of the cooking. · Chuka soba: relatively thin, springy straight noodles in a soy-based broth drawn from pork bone and chicken (豚骨・鶏ガラ), topped with sweet pork back-fat (背脂) that floats on the surface. The clean, delicate dashi is carried by the strength of the soy tare, so a bowl that looks rich eats surprisingly light. The shop is known for slicing its big chashu fresh to order.
places.gfd: A classic wheat-noodle chuka soba: the noodles are wheat, the soy tare is almost certainly wheat-based shoyu, and the broth uses pork and chicken. No gluten-free menu, no published allergen handling, and no indication of any wheat-free preparation. Not safe for a celiac diner.
places.vgd: This is a traditional Kyoto chuka-soba shop whose single signature bowl is built on a pork-bone and chicken (豚骨・鶏ガラ) broth finished with sweet pork back-fat (背脂) and a soy tare. The menu centers on this one animal-based ramen, so there is no vegan option. A plant-based diner cannot eat here.
places.hours: Tuesday-Friday 11:00-15:00; closed Monday, Saturday, Sunday. Closes early when the day's noodles/ingredients run out. Note: some guides list a longer through-service window of 11:00-18:00 until sell-out; the shop sells out frequently, so arriving early is advised.

places.chef: Zakoya group (seafood restaurant group) · Kyoto · Mentomeshi Zakoya is part of the Zakoya group (ZACOYA), a Kyoto seafood-focused hospitality brand running a cluster of fish-centric restaurants around Karasuma, Sanjo and Gion. The ramen concept began at a Hyakumanben main store and a Gion branch; both have since closed, and the shop relocated to its current Higashidoin-Rokkaku spot near Karasuma-Oike in February 2024. · A deliberately meat-free take on ramen: the whole bowl is built from the sea rather than pork or chicken, staying true to the Zakoya group's fish-forward identity. places.gfd: This is a wheat-noodle ramen shop with house-made noodles, and the tare is almost certainly wheat-based soy sauce. The broth is fish-based rather than pork, but the noodles and tare make the bowl unsafe for gluten avoidance.
places.vgd: Despite being meat-free (no pork or chicken), every dish is built on fish and seafood — dashi from sea bream, scallop, ribbonfish and dried sardines, with fish toppings and a seasoned egg. Not vegan or vegetarian.

places.notes: This is the sohonten — the original headquarters — of Tenkaippin, the cult chicken-broth ramen chain that began in Kyoto. In November 1971, founder Tsutomu Kimura, having lost his job when the gallery company he worked for went bankrupt, had a friend build him a ramen cart out of
places.chef: 木村勉 (Tsutomu Kimura) · founder · Kyoto · This is the sohonten — the original headquarters — of Tenkaippin, the cult chicken-broth ramen chain that began in Kyoto. In November 1971, founder Tsutomu Kimura, having lost his job when the gallery company he worked for went bankrupt, had a friend build him a ramen cart out of scrap metal and started pulling a yatai (food cart) around the Ginkaku-ji area. On opening night he reportedly sold only 11 bowls. He kept experimenting, and after three years and nine months he perfected the now-legendary kotteri broth. With the goodwill of a stone-mason whose lot he was using, the cart was fixed in place and grew into his first storefront in August 1975 — on this Ichijoji site, which remains the chain's spiritual home. · Kimura's idea was a broth that is 'eaten, not drunk' — a slow-cooked chicken-and-vegetable kotteri so concentrated it behaves like a sauce. The beef-tendon special was developed personally by the chairman over many trial batches, balancing the sweet-savory tendon to harmonize with that signature soup, and the recipe is kept exclusive to the sohonten. · The signature is the kotteri (こってり) bowl: a thick, almost potage-like broth si…
places.gfd: Not celiac-safe. The kotteri broth is built on chicken bones and vegetables, but the ramen is served with standard wheat noodles and a wheat-based shoyu tare, and the kitchen also fries gyoza, karaage and other wheat items in shared equipment. No gluten-free noodles, broth, or accommodation is offered, and there is no dedicated fryer. A celiac diner cannot eat the ramen here.
places.vgd: Not suitable for vegans. The signature broth is a long-simmered chicken-bone (鶏ガラ) and vegetable kotteri base, and the flagship-only specials are beef-tendon (牛すじ) ramen and pork rice (豚重). There are no plant-based broth, noodle, or topping options.
places.hours: 11:00-1:00 the next day (L.O. 0:45, 15 min before closing). No regular closing day (closed only on New Year's Day).

places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto · A husband-and-wife team who began as a pop-up in the Fukakusa area, running for about three months before opening this permanent shop near Toji Station in January 2021, taking over a former Chinese-restaurant space in Minami Ward. The couple draw on their own experience raising children to run a warm, family-friendly counter. · The name itself is the philosophy: to thoroughly and patiently slow-simmer the chicken. The owners describe themselves as still refining the recipe, treating the bowl as a work in continual improvement. · An exceptionally concentrated chicken paitan (torigara hakutou) — the signature 'Tokoton Tori'. Chicken and a generous amount of vegetables are simmered thoroughly and gently for a long time (the literal meaning of the shop's name) into a broth so thick a ladle can stand upright in it. It is rich in collagen — enough that it sets when cooled — yet the vegetables keep the finish surprisingly clean rather than heavy. Flat noodles from Kyoto noodle maker Teikaku cling to the dense soup; sets pair the bowl with a donburi of house-made chashu, scallion, egg yolk and fried-onion shrimp oil, and fish-powder, chili and mazesoba variations are …
places.gfd: Not gluten-free. The ramen uses wheat noodles (from Kyoto noodle maker Teikaku/棣鄂) and the broth is built on chicken and vegetables with a typical tare; donburi sets add chashu and other components. No gluten-free menu, dedicated prep, or allergen accommodation is mentioned by any source. Treat as unsafe for celiac diners; ask in person if highly sensitive.
places.vgd: Not vegan or vegetarian. The signature bowl is a chicken-based paitan broth (chicken simmered with vegetables); donburi sets include house-made chashu, egg yolk and shrimp oil. Although a large quantity of vegetables goes into the broth, it is fundamentally animal-based. No vegan or vegetarian option is offered.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] Before opening his own shop, the owner spent roughly ten years training at one of Kyoto's most storied ramen institutions, Shinpuku Saikan (新福菜館) at Takabashi — the legendary home of jet-black soy chuka soba. He carries that Kyoto rich-soy lineage forward while adding his own ref
places.chef: owner-chef · Opened in 2020 in the Kuze district of Kyoto's Minami-ku, on the edge of Mukou City near JR Mukomachi Station. · Before opening his own shop, the owner spent roughly ten years training at one of Kyoto's most storied ramen institutions, Shinpuku Saikan (新福菜館) at Takabashi — the legendary home of jet-black soy chuka soba. He carries that Kyoto rich-soy lineage forward while adding his own refinements. · All vegetables and ingredients are domestically sourced, and the broth itself is the product of constant tinkering — described on the shop's own site as a rich-soy soup 'developed through improvement upon improvement' to land on a deep flavor with a light, clean finish. · The flagship bowl is the 醤油中華そば (rich-soy chuka soba), a concentrated pork-bone-and-soy broth that drinks surprisingly clean, finished with Kyoto's prized Kujo green onions. Other draws include the 宇宙一のまぜそば ("best-in-the-universe" maze soba), 濃厚担々麺, the vegetable-laden 京都タンメン, and a much-loved fried-rice set.
places.gfd: This is a traditional Kyoto-style rich-soy chuka soba shop. places.chef: owner · Tokyo / Higashi-Ikebukuro Taishoken lineage, adapted for Kyoto · This is a Kyoto branch of the legendary 東池袋大勝軒, the Tokyo shop in the Higashi-Ikebukuro district credited as the birthplace of tsukemen. The dish was born by accident in the 1950s: while working at the original shop, owner Kazuo Yamagishi would eat noodles dipped in broth, zaru-soba style, as a quick staff meal; a regular customer saw it and asked to try the same, and from 1955 it joined the menu as tsukemen. · A defining Kyoto touch: because tsukemen began as a staff meal meant to be eaten fast, the dipping broth was traditionally served only lukewarm, but here it is served piping hot for local tastes. The dip is lighter and a touch sweeter than today's intensely thick tsukemen, loaded with chashu, menma and narutomaki, with seafood aromatics that bloom when you add soup to the leftover broth at the end. · Tsukemen (dipping noodles) — chewy, thick-cut wheat noodles served alongside a sweet-leaning dipping broth that blends chicken bones, pork bones and seafood. The signature pair is the 元祖つけ麺 (original) and the 濃厚つけ麺 (rich, finished with fish powder); an atsumori option serves the noodles piping hot.
places.gfd: Tsukemen and ramen built on thick wheat noodles, with a chicken-pork-seafood dipping broth that is almost certainly seasoned with wheat-based shoyu tare. places.chef: owner-operated specialty ramen shop · Shizuoka, then Machida (Tokyo), now Fukakusa, Kyoto · Katsukyo began in Shizuoka in October 2006, opened a second shop in Machida, Tokyo in June 2017, and brought the operation to its current spot in Fukakusa — on Shidan-dori between Fushimi Inari and Ryukoku University — in October 2019. places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto · The owner took up ramen seriously later in life, studying the craft on his own after turning 50, and opened this small shop in a quiet Kitashirakawa residential corner (near Chayama Station on the Eizan line, just south of the famous Ichijoji ramen district) on October 14, 2021. Despite the weathered, old-fashioned lantern signage that makes it look like a decades-old institution, it is a relatively new arrival. · He set out simply to become the neighborhood's beloved ramen shop, building bowls on pure chicken stock with female local chicken and refusing to muddy the soup. Offering a plain kake ramen for just 500 yen is read as quiet confidence in the broth and noodles alone. · Chicken-forward ramen made entirely from poultry stock. The clear shoyu chuka-soba is the chef's calling card, with a clean, transparent broth and medium-straight noodles, while the rich tori-paitan (chicken white broth) is praised as so deep it tastes almost like it contains pork bones. The Half & Half pairs a transparent shoyu seitan broth beneath the creamy chicken paitan in a single bowl that grows richer as you stir.

places.vgd: Every bowl is built on chicken broth (the shop uses female local chicken bones), with pork chashu, and the broth/tare contain animal products throughout. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered.

places.chef: owner-chef · Kyoto, Japan · Kinzan opened in 2013 in the quiet Nishioji-Shichijo residential pocket of Shimogyo-ku, a roughly 15-minute walk from JR Nishioji Station. The owner trained at the respected Takabashi Ramen before striking out on his own, and the shop has since grown into a local favorite popular enough to open a second branch near Kyoto City Hall (Shiyakusho-mae). · A Kyoto-rooted approach: classic local-style tonkotsu-shoyu done with carefully chosen regional ingredients (Kyotanba/Kyoto Highland pork from Hiyoshi Farm, Kujo negi, aged soy from the Koyama and Goko breweries, Kondo noodles), cooked in an open kitchen so guests can watch the bowl come together. · The signature bowl is a 'Kyoto black shoyu' (京都黒醤油) ramen: a glossy, near-jet-black soup built on a pork-bone base, given sharpness and depth by aged soy sauce and a mellow sweetness by back fat. It is finished with two styles of Kyoto Highland pork chashu (lean and fatty, torched to order), Kujo green onion, bean sprouts, menma, and a slick of back fat. Straight medium-thin noodles from the long-established Kondo Seimen give a firm, wheaty bite.

places.chef: Sakakimoto · owner, chef · This is the second outpost of the Jun chicken-paitan brand, following the original near Marutamachi; it opened in the Shijo-Karasuma area on August 13, 2025. · Owner Sakakimoto came to ramen the long way around, spending some fifteen years training in kappo (Japanese fine-dining) and sushi kitchens before striking out on his own. That fine-dining grounding shows in every detail of the bowl. · Sakakimoto has said that if he was going to open his own place, he wanted to do something only he could do — hence the labor-intensive, single-serving emulsified broth and the kappo-trained attention to finish and presentation. · The signature is a tori-paitan (chicken white-soup) soba in an espuma-like, foamed broth. Rather than ladling from one big pot, the kitchen emulsifies the chicken soup bowl by bowl in a blender, whipping it into a mild, airy, almost cappuccino-like froth. The base is built primarily on Kagoshima chicken, rounded out with small amounts of Miyazaki and Oita pork bones, and paired with custom medium-thick, chewy noodles and rare pork chashu.

places.vgd: Every bowl is built on an animal base: a rich chicken (tori-paitan) broth made primarily with Kagoshima chicken, supplemented with Miyazaki and Oita pork bones, and topped with rare pork chashu. places.chef: ramen shop, izakaya offshoot · Kyoto · Toyojiro opened on December 1, 2024 in the Kawaramachi/Kiyamachi area of Kyoto (Yaoyacho, Nakagyo-ku), growing out of the popular tuna-and-wagyu izakaya Toyota (とよ田) and sharing its premises. places.vgd: A Jiro-style ramen shop built around a beef-fat broth (rendered fat from 48-month-old female cattle), wheat noodles, and beef-tendon (bokkake) toppings. There is no vegan or vegetarian bowl here; the entire concept is meat-forward, so a plant-based diner has nothing safe to order.

places.chef: Miyaji Tamotsu · Cantonese kitchen, tantanmen specialist, family-run · Muko City (Teradocho), Kyoto · Kirin-en opened in 1967, when authentic Cantonese cooking was still a rarity in the then-farmland district of Muko. Founder Miyaji Tamotsu (宮路保) set out to let local residents enjoy genuine Guangdong cuisine casually, and the place has stayed family-run, with Miyaji Ryo (宮路亮) now serving as store manager. · The house motto for its spicy dishes is 「辛くて旨い」— 'spicy but delicious' (うま辛) — chasing flavor and craft rather than heat for its own sake. · A fiery tantanmen built on four kinds of chili plus a house-made meat-miso for depth, which became the restaurant's calling card during Muko City's spicy-food (gekikara) town-revitalization push. places.chef: owner-chef (former Sugichiyo head cook) · Tokiwa (near Uzumasa), Ukyo-ku, Kyoto · Opened in 2002 by a chef who had headed the kitchen (店長／元料理長) at Sugichiyo (杉千代), a legendary Uzumasa ramen shop that drew lines for its then-revolutionary bowls some two decades ago. places.chef: owner · 麺屋 月 is a small abura-soba specialist that opened on February 22, 2026 in Kyoto's Shimogamo neighborhood, on Kitaoji-dori near Kyoto Prefectural University in what is a competitive local ramen district. It is an intimate spot of about seven tables seating roughly fourteen guests. · The shop leans on quality where it counts: the thick noodles come from Menya Teigaku, a venerable Kyoto noodle maker founded in 1931, and the abura-soba is built to be enjoyed first as-is, then re-seasoned partway through with chili oil and vinegar to change the flavor. · The signature bowl is abura-soba (brothless mixed noodles): extra-thick noodles tossed in a house-made sweet-and-spicy shoyu tare and fragrant aroma oil, finished with chashu or stewed pork belly (kakuni), menma, soft-boiled egg, shredded nori and white negi. Portions step up generously by weight, from 200g up to 500g for the same modest price band.
places.gfd: This is an abura-soba and ramen shop: the noodles are wheat (made by long-established Kyoto noodle maker Menya Teigaku) and the signature dish is dressed in a house sweet-spicy soy (shoyu) tare, which is wheat-based. There is no published gluten-free menu or any allergen accommodation. Not suitable for celiac diners.
places.vgd: The menu centers on abura-soba topped with pork chashu and stewed pork (kakuni), plus chicken-broth and dashi (fish/seafood) noodle bowls and Okayama-style fried chicken. No vegan or vegetarian option is advertised.
places.hours: 11:00-14:30, 17:00-1:30 the next day (irregular days off, closures announced on Instagram)

places.chef: 樹下真一 (Kinoshita, aka 'Sadakazu') · owner-operator · Kyoto (Gion, Higashiyama-ku); relocated from Fushimi-ku, Kyoto. · Sadakazu is a late-night Gion institution that earned the nickname "幻のラーメン" (phantom ramen) because it opens only for about three hours after 10 p.m. and often sells out after roughly 35 bowls. It is a solo-run six-seat counter. · The broth is a mellow soy flavoring with deep umami — a back-fat 'seabura chaccha' style that stays drinkable rather than heavy ('背脂ちゃっちゃ系だが、そんなに油はきつくない。まろやかな醤油ダシ'), the kind of bowl meant to cap off a night out in Gion. · Its signature is a Kyoto-style back-fat soy-sauce ramen (背脂醤油ラーメン, 'seabura chaccha'): a clean chicken-bone shoyu broth blanketed with pork back-fat, paired with thin, low-hydration straight noodles and chashu (¥700). places.gfd: Not gluten-free and not celiac-safe. The bowl uses thin, low-hydration straight wheat noodles in a soy-sauce (shoyu) tare that almost certainly contains wheat, plus a chicken/pork broth. There is no gluten-free menu, no dedicated equipment, and no allergy information published. This is a tiny single-owner late-night counter shop and should be treated as unsafe for anyone avoiding gluten.
places.vgd: No vegan options. The signature bowl is built on a chicken-bone soy-sauce (shoyu) broth finished with pork back-fat (seabura) and chashu pork, so it is fundamentally animal-based. No vegetable or vegan ramen is offered, and no sources indicate any plant-based accommodation. A vegan diner has nothing suitable here.

It is built for the after-hours crowd, opening into the evening and running deep into the night for diners winding down after an evening out in one of Kyoto's most storied entertainment districts. · An accessible, comforting bowl tuned for late-night Gion: a clean, drinkable broth rather than a heavy one, finished to each diner's liking with the condiments on the counter. · The signature bowl is the 特選醤油ラーメン (special soy-sauce ramen): a light, easy-drinking Kyoto-style shoyu broth with just a touch of back fat and a gently restrained soy depth, served with medium-thick noodles, thin slices of pork loin, flavorful menma, and white and green onions. places.chef: Saifullah · owner · Kyoto · Ayam-YA grew out of a ramen company whose very first shop opened not in Japan but in Seattle. When the team brought the concept home to Japan's hyper-competitive ramen scene, they struggled to draw crowds, until an Indonesian exchange student asked a simple question that changed everything: 'Do you use only chicken?' That was the moment the founders learned that many visitors could not eat ordinary ramen for religious reasons. Determined to let Muslim travelers in Kyoto enjoy a real bowl of Japanese ramen with peace of mind, they reformulated the recipe and pursued halal certification through the Malaysia Halal Corporation. 'Ayam' means 'chicken' in Indonesian and Malay. · Make a genuinely delicious Japanese ramen that observant Muslims and curious travelers alike can eat with peace of mind, by keeping the kitchen free of pork and alcohol and building flavor honestly from chicken rather than additives. · Tori-paitan (rich chicken) ramen served as the basic shoyu (soy) chicken soba and a richer shio (salt) chicken bowl, with miso also offered; the broths lean on chicken with a seafood aroma for depth, finished with finely minced onion and scallion, and m…
places.gfd: This is a standard ramen and tsukemen shop built on wheat noodles, with shoyu, shio and miso bowls whose tare typically contains wheat-based soy sauce. No gluten-free noodle or gluten-free preparation is advertised, so it is not suitable for celiac diners. Halal does not mean gluten-free.
places.vgd: The house style is tori-paitan (rich chicken broth) and the signature bowls are chicken-based, so the standard menu is not vegan or vegetarian. The kitchen is halal (no pork, no alcohol) and avoids chemical seasonings, which makes it ingredient-conscious, but a plant-based diner would need to ask directly whether anything meat-free can be prepared and should not assume a vegan option exists.

places.chef: machi-chuka diner, local lunch and dinner spot · Nishikyogoku, Kyoto · A neighborhood machi-chuka (Japanese-style Chinese) restaurant that has fed the Nishikyogoku district for roughly 40 years, just east of Hankyu Nishikyogoku Station on Hanayacho-dori. It draws a cross-section of locals, from solo diners on their lunch break to families, in a bright, big-windowed room with a warm, unpretentious feel. · Honest, generous, affordable home-style Chinese cooking for the neighborhood — big portions, courteous service, and prices that keep regulars coming back day after day. · The signature bowl is the maabo-tenshinhan (mapo Tianjin rice): a fluffy egg over rice blanketed in a generous, glossy mapo sauce. The sauce is built on house-made fermented black bean paste (豆鼓醤) and several chili pastes with ginger and plenty of garlic, given depth by coarsely minced salted fermented black beans (豆鼓の粒) and finished with house chili oil, with finely minced pork for richness — kept addictively savory rather than punishingly hot, served around 1,050 yen with soup and pickles.
places.gfd: No gluten-free provision. This is a Japanese-style Chinese diner built on wheat: noodles, gyoza wrappers, and sauces thickened/seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce and likely doubanjiang. The signature mapo Tianjin rice rides on a mapo sauce that almost certainly contains wheat soy seasoning. There is no indication of gluten-free menus, dedicated equipment, or allergen handling. Not suitable for celiacs.
places.vgd: No vegan offering. The kitchen is meat- and seafood-forward: pork features in the mapo sauce, gyoza, fried chicken, and broths; dishes use animal-based stocks. Even otherwise plant-leaning items (fried rice, ankake) are cooked with meat/egg and shared woks. No vegetarian or vegan menu is advertised.

places.notes: [Mom & Pop] A small, refined Sichuan-leaning Chinese kitchen tucked into a quiet stretch of Nijo-dori just south of the Imperial Palace, opened in 2013 and run single-handedly by its chef-owner. He came up through the produce markets before cooking, and that background shows in his sourcing
places.chef: owner, chef · Kyoto (Nakagyo-ku, Gosho-minami / Karasuma-Oike area) · A small, refined Sichuan-leaning Chinese kitchen tucked into a quiet stretch of Nijo-dori just south of the Imperial Palace, opened in 2013 and run single-handedly by its chef-owner. He came up through the produce markets before cooking, and that background shows in his sourcing — a cook with a reliable eye for ingredients who keeps the menu deliberately compact. · Keep the cooking simple and let quality ingredients carry it — the kind of place where, as one chef put it, everything you order somehow tastes good. Heat is balanced and aromatic rather than punishing. · Sichuan-style cooking pitched a notch upscale rather than fiery for its own sake: a fragrant tantanmen (the lunchtime dry 汁なし version is especially praised), a mapo tofu where the Sichuan pepper and chili oil are rounded out by the sweetness of the ground pork, plus boiled dumplings and sweet-and-sour pork.
places.gfd: A Sichuan Chinese kitchen built around wheat. The tantanmen and dumpling skins are wheat-flour, the chili/sesame tare and seasonings used in dishes like the mapo tofu lean on soy-based and bean-paste condiments that typically contain wheat, and there is no gluten-free menu or protocol. Not suitable for celiacs. A coeliac diner could ask whether any single rice- or vegetable-based plate could be prepared plainly, but cross-contact in a one-cook wok kitchen is unavoidable — treat as not GF-safe.
places.vgd: Not a vegan specialist. The signature bowls (tantanmen, mapo tofu, boiled dumplings, sweet-and-sour pork) all use pork and/or animal-derived broth and condiments. There is no marked vegan option. Because it is a small a-la-carte Sichuan kitchen run by one chef, a vegan might be able to ask in advance for a plain vegetable stir-fry, but nothing is confirmed plant-based, so reserve and ask directly…
places.hours: Dinner 18:00-21:00 (L.O. ~20:30). Lunch not currently served (as of recent listing). Closed Sunday; Monday occasionally closed (~twice monthly); irregular temporary closures possible.

places.chef: owner · 大阪（人類みな麺類系列） · Ramen Daisenso ("Ramen World War") is the Kyoto outpost of the acclaimed Osaka ramen group behind Jinrui Mina Menrui, the much-queued shop that turned shoyu ramen into something theatrical. This branch opened in October 2022 on the first floor of a renovated Kawaramachi building (formerly a sushi restaurant) and marked the group's first move into Kyoto. · A noodle-first house: the noodle-making room is visible from the street, signalling pride in house-made noodles, paired with generous service — diners can add up to five chashu slices and get a free half-portion noodle refill (kaedama). · The flagship bowl is the Kansai-dashi shoyu ramen named 'Pistol' (ピストル) — a clear, light-bodied shoyu broth built on Nagoya Cochin chicken bones and scallop, with deep umami and a faint natural sweetness. places.vgd: All four signature bowls are animal-based: the broths are made from chicken bones (Nagoya Cochin), scallop, and fish/dashi elements, and chashu (pork) is a centerpiece. No vegan or vegetarian ramen is offered.

places.chef: old-established independent late-night ramen counter · 博多長浜ラーメン みよし opened in 1983 (昭和58年) in Kyoto's Kiyamachi/Sanjo entertainment district and has become an old-school local institution — '京都の人間でその名を知らぬ者はいない' (there is no one in Kyoto who doesn't know its name). For roughly four decades it has carried the same Hakata Nagahama taste, its small open counter running late into the night. · A purist, no-frills tonkotsu shop: keep the pork-bone broth going, add nothing unnecessary, and let each diner build their own flavor with the tabletop condiments. Regulars even treat certain moves (like adding pepper or curry powder) as 'forbidden,' and finishing by pouring extra broth over rice is part of the ritual. · Essentially one bowl done one way: Hakata Nagahama-style tonkotsu ramen — a clean, gently sweet pork-bone broth paired with ultra-thin Hakata straight noodles. Diners customize at the table with around eleven free toppings (beni-shoga pickled ginger, coarse ichimi chili, tenkasu tempura scraps, sesame, etc.) and can order kaedama noodle refills, which is treated as part of doing Nagahama ramen 'your way.'
places.gfd: This is a Hakata-style tonkotsu ramen shop built around wheat noodles (ultra-thin Hakata straight noodles) in a pork-bone broth, with kaedama (noodle refills) as a core part of the experience. places.chef: Independently operated local Chinese restaurant / 町中華, Part of the small 龍門 group in Kyoto · Kyoto (Sichuan-style Chinese cooking). · 龍門 is a small Kyoto chain of authentic Sichuan / neighborhood-Chinese (町中華) restaurants run by 株式会社長城, with the Honten near Sanjo-Higashioji and branches in Okazaki and here in Uzumasa, in Ukyo-ku near the Arashiyama (Randen) line and JR Uzumasa. places.chef: owner-operator · Ono, Yamashina-ku, Kyoto · Iwasaki Tanmen opened its doors on March 1, 2023 in the Ono neighborhood of Yamashina, just steps from Ono Station, taking over a storefront that previously housed another ramen shop (Shioemon). It is a rarity in Kyoto: a shop devoted to tanmen, a vegetable-piled salt ramen far more common in the Kanto region of eastern Japan than here in Kansai. · Make-it-your-own simplicity: diners can dial the vegetables, pork, noodle quantity, garlic and spice to taste, and garlic is served on the side so each guest controls their own portion. It arrives looking hearty and Jiro-esque, yet the soup is surprisingly clean and light, with no heavy back-fat. A pot of house chili-miso (kara-miso) sits at hand so you can stir in heat and depth gradually as you eat.

places.chef: Inoue (proprietor) · owner, chef · Ichijoji, Sakyo-ku, Kyoto — on the city's famous Ichijoji ramen street, but a deliberate step away from the heavy-broth pack. · The shop is the latest evolution of a Kyoto noodle maker who has spent years chasing dashi rather than richness. places.notes: [Meat kaiseki · Gion, a self-taught owner's all-wagyu counter] A two-storey wooden house a step off Hanamikoji, reached down a narrow path between textured earthen walls, with eight seats at a hinoki counter (renovated in 2023). Owner Tsutomu Ito came to meat through a friend who graded beef and a first taste of beef butchered that same day, is self-taught as a cook, and opened in the owner's home town of Gion at the end of 2004 under the family name Miyoshi; the building had been the owner's mother's salon. One course a month runs through a dozen beef dishes — tongue cured on kombu, beef sashimi, shabu-shabu, steak and sukiyaki — between seasonal seafood and vegetables, and ends with rice and egg yolk. Tabelog Award 2026 Silver; a 2026 reviewer notes a Michelin star from 2018 to 2022. Upstairs is a one-group inn where diners can eat and then sleep. Expect ¥60,000–75,000 plus service; one July 2026 diner felt regulars got more attention.

places.notes: [Kappo · Higashiyama, a ryotei-trained chef's playful counter] A second-floor counter of nine near Higashiyama station, where owner-chef Tsukasa Miyashita, from Mie and trained for sixteen years at Gion Maruyama and Gion Sasaki, cooks Japanese food with turns no one else takes: fried ayu wrapped in fresh spring rolls, a dried-Matsutake soup with a Chinese edge, an autumn "parfait" of tofu sauce and dashi jelly, rice served as sushi, as egg-on-rice and as mapo. Opened in 2021 with Yuumei Hongo, it holds a star in the Michelin Guide Kyoto Osaka 2026 (per 2026 reviews) and Tabelog's 2026 Bronze. Everyone starts at 18:00; the room is lively, and a July 2026 diner was greeted at the door by the chef. Course ¥30,250 plus service; closed Sundays and Mondays.

places.notes: [Kappo · Higashiyama, a forager's "museum of food" opposite Shoren-in] Across the lane from the gate of Shoren-in, behind a plaque reading Shun Gyuan and a tea-house approach, eight seats face a tatami-topped counter, an okudo stove and shelves of antique jars. Owner Masanori Tsukioka, from Hokkaido, began cooking at 15 in Sapporo, trained around Japan including under Hisao Nakahigashi at Kusakui Nakahigashi, ran Jimi Kougetsu in Kusatsu, and moved to the United States in 2019 to open a restaurant, but COVID ended the plan and the chef restarted in Kyoto, opening here in 2021. The course follows what the chef picks in Ohara and Miyama: a hassun like a summer meadow, white-miso soups, Akashi conger eel, 50-day aged beef from Sakaeya in Kusatsu, handmade 100% buckwheat soba and stove-cooked rice. Tabelog Award 2026 Bronze and Japanese cuisine WEST 100. Lunch ¥15,000, dinner ¥30,000; closed Tuesdays, Wednesdays and the last day of the month.

places.notes: [Italian · Shogoin, a Kyoto-born chef's Italian in a century-old house] Near Heian Shrine, down a narrow entrance and stairs that one diner likened to entering a cave, a renovated house of over 100 years with walls of twisted Meiji-style brickwork, Wajima lacquer and Kyoto ceramics on the table. Chef Ken Sakamoto, born in Kyoto in 1975, fell for Italian food on a university trip, trained at Il Papparaldo and spent nine years as head chef of Il Giottone before opening here in 2014. The courses pair Kyoto vegetables with fish and meat in surprising ways — prosciutto with mango and dosa, a hamo soup like tom yum — and the meal ends with cenci, the fried pastry that gives the shop its name; a vegan plate has appeared mid-course. Michelin Guide Kyoto Osaka 2026 one star (per 2026 reviews), Tabelog Award 2026 Bronze. Weekday lunch is ¥12,100; one October 2026 diner found the explanations hurried.

places.notes: [Tea kaiseki · Maruyama Park, a Kyoto master's one-sitting counter] At the far end of Maruyama Park, beyond Yasaka Shrine, fourteen guests sit at one counter and start together at 18:00 for about three hours of tea kaiseki. The owner, Hitoshi Ishihara (石原仁司), born in Shimane in 1952, began training at 15 at a famous Osaka restaurant, rose to head chef in Kyoto at 24, and opened Mizai in 2004; a June 2026 reviewer recalls three Michelin stars many times over. The name is a Zen phrase: the way is never finished. The evening opens with the etiquette of a tea meal, then relaxes; it runs through a lavish sashimi course, a grand hassun, a scorched-rice tea porridge and an astonishing fruit course, and ends with matcha the owner whisks. No food photos. ¥65,000 plus tax and service, cash preferred; book by phone up to a year ahead.

places.notes: [Kaiseki · Gion, a family kaiseki house since 1945] Through a simple noren and a stone-paved passage in the middle of Gion, a long, polished hinoki counter of twelve and a sunken-kotatsu room at the back. The restaurant was founded in 1945; the chef now is Kanji Kubota, born in Kyoto Prefecture in 1976, who trained in Tokyo and came home to take over from the chef's father, who still appears now and then. The cooking is quiet and seasonal — hamo in summer, Matsutake dobin-mushi in autumn, a hassun on artists' tableware — and lunch is ¥13,200. New guests are called by name, and in September 2026 an apprentice explained dishes in fluent English to overseas diners. Tabelog Bronze or Silver every year since 2019 and Japanese cuisine WEST 100. Closed Sundays.

places.notes: [Suppon · Kamigyo, a 340-year-old turtle house] An Edo-period building on a quiet street near Senbon-dori, with a courtyard and tatami rooms, where one family has served a single dish for about 340 years and eighteen generations, by diners' accounts since the Genroku era. Sword marks said to be left by samurai remain at the entrance (July 2026), and reviewers note that writers such as Yasunari Kawabata and Naoya Shiga were patrons. The course never changes: turtle jelly, the bubbling marunabe of turtle, sake, soy sauce and ginger served twice, then a rich rice porridge with mochi and egg. Fans call it odourless and deeply savoury; one 2026 diner found the repeated pot monotonous, another the pace brisk. ¥26,000 all in; no children; parking for six.

places.notes: [Kaiseki · Ginkaku-ji, a forager's kitchen of wild plants and stove-cooked rice] At the foot of the approach to Ginkaku-ji, a counter of twelve and two upstairs tatami rooms where the course is whatever Hisao Nakahigashi found that morning in Ohara: shoots, leaves, flowers and seeds, in a hassun laid out like a hillside, soups and plainly grilled dishes. Born in Kyoto Prefecture in 1952 and raised at Miyamasou, the inn in Hanase known for tsumikusa (foraged-plant) cooking, the owner trained there, served as its head chef and opened here in 1997; the rice, cooked in an okudo-san wood stove and served with grilled dried sardines, became the main event after the 1993 rice shortage. The site reports a Michelin Green Star for its sustainable approach. Diners love the chef's jokes at the counter; book by phone from 8:00 on the 1st of the month before. Lunch from ¥12,100, dinner from ¥24,200 all in.

In the 1993 rice shortage a clay rice pot from Ichishiro-gama in Hikone led to the house style with plain white rice as the main dish. Every morning the owner goes to Ohara to gather wild plants and seasonal produce (Tabelog; official site). places.notes: [Kaiseki · Anekoji, tea-kaiseki cooking on Rosanjin ware] A Sukiya-style house from the early Showa era, once a tea-utensil shop, left almost as it was: a broad entrance, a small inner garden, a counter of five or six and a four-and-a-half-mat room down the corridor. Chef Shinichi Iida, who trained in Kanazawa and Kyoto, has haunted antique shops since apprentice days, and the course comes on pieces by Rosanjin and Eiraku alongside Taisho glass. The cooking keeps to the shape of tea kaiseki — eel Yawata-maki in May, a hamo and ume soup in June, Matsutake in autumn — and reviewers call the clear soups the measure of the place. No photos of the food, cash only, and nearly every seat goes to regulars and their guests. Tabelog Gold every year from 2019 to 2026.

places.notes: [Kaiseki · Yasaka-dori, a showman's Kyoto kaiseki] Up steps on Yasaka-dori south of Kennin-ji, past guardian figures at the door, thirteen guests at a counter with a big charcoal grill in the middle watch a crew of apprentices and chef Hiroshi Sasaki work, and everyone starts together. The chef buys at markets and fishing ports and serves the day's best with wit and some theatre: abalone porridge, a cutlassfish so big it is called a dragon, sushi handed across the counter, a dessert of corn tempura. Born in Nara in 1961 into a family of cooks, the chef ran Fujita in Pontocho at 27 and opened Gion Sasaki in 1998, moving here in 2006; 2026 reviewers note seven straight years of three Michelin stars. places.notes: [Kaiseki · Higashiyama, a warm chef's sukiya house below Yasaka Shrine] Down a stone-paved lane between Yasaka Shrine and Kodaiji, a sukiya-style house of bamboo and hinoki with a single-slab counter 7.5 metres long and a small garden visible from every room. Owner-chef Masayoshi Nishikawa, born in Kyoto in 1975 to a family of Yuzen dyers, trained at Gion Sasaki, ran the kitchen at Warabi no Sato, and opened here in 2009; a Michelin listing followed within a year, and 2026 reviewers count two stars for fifteen years running. The menu changes daily: dashi from Yasaka Shrine's soft spring water, Ohara vegetables, a pressed mackerel sushi diners rave about, and touches like caviar on grilled eggplant. Reviewers love the chef's jokes and send-offs; in September 2026 the chef was running the kitchen almost alone, with an apprentice joining in October.

places.notes: [Kaiseki · Gion, tea-ceremony cooking at a friendly counter] Through a noren and down a water-sprinkled stone alley off Hanamikoji, a hinoki counter of ten looks onto a small garden, with tatami rooms upstairs set with fine tableware. Chef Nobuhiko Masuda, born in Shiga in 1957, spent twenty years at the ryotei Shofukuro, opened Sangencha in Mizuguchi, Shiga, and moved to Gion; the cooking keeps the spirit of Zen cuisine and the tea meal while playing with ideas like mascarpone soy sauce for the sashimi. Courses end with rice from the chef's home town, as much as you like, and a melting mizu-yokan. Regulars come back for years for the chef's gentle humour; families are welcome, with a kids' menu. Lunch from about ¥10,000. Closed Tuesdays.

Owner-chef Tadashi Takayama went to Italy at 22, came home defeated by the language, went back at 27 to cook in Piedmont and Tuscany, and was sous-chef at Crescios in Campania before opening here in 2019. The course is about 25 bites built for fun as well as flavour: a juice wrapped in white chocolate with the menu as a printed QR code, Miyazaki caviar on squid-ink crisps, foie gras choux, a risotto of Seiko crab. Plan on three hours and come hungry. Many guests are from overseas, and staff are young and warm. ¥30,000 all in, plus ¥1,000 for water; closed Mondays.

places.notes: [Innovative · Higashiyama, Nordic-Japanese cooking over open fire] A townhouse more than 250 years old, a minute from Higashiyama station, where ten guests at the counter watch the cooks work a wood fire and oven. Chef Jacob Kear, born in California and raised in Japan, cooked at Noma in Copenhagen and Noma Tokyo and was head chef of Clooney in New Zealand; drinks come from Yusuke Sakaibe, a cocktail champion the chef met in New Zealand. The name is Basque for earth, the ring a moon. Courses mix Nordic fermentation with Japanese seasons and Ohara vegetables — sea urchin manju, Biwa trout roasted in the fireplace with clam chowder sauce, fried ice-cream doughnuts to finish. A 2026 review reports a Michelin star in the Kyoto Osaka 2026 guide. In August a casual walk-in lunch runs for a few weeks. Book online; closed Sundays and Mondays.

places.notes: [Kaiseki · Gion, a tea-kaiseki counter with a big heart] Through a lattice door off Hanamikoji and along a stone path: a calm counter of eight and private rooms. The owner-chef, who ran the kitchen of a long-established inn before opening here in 2015, cooks about thirteen courses in the spirit of tea kaiseki on made-to-order pottery — a crab-only sushi roll, mackerel with its own liver sauce, Ishigaki beef in a hot pot, rice with Lake Biwa eel. Tabelog says it has held two Michelin stars since 2016. Diners find the chef imposing at first and warm once you settle; the staff chat and send you off with walking tips. Bookings are for two or more, and first-timers must book online. Lunch from ¥20,000. A casual sister, また吉, serves lunch, shaved ice and Italian nearby.

places.notes: [Kaiseki · Shimogamo, a master's tea-style kaiseki by the Tadasu no Mori] Beside the ancient woods of Shimogamo Shrine, a 455 m² compound with counter seats, three private rooms and a tea room, "Suishoan", moved here from a 1935 building, all hung with scrolls and flowers chosen by the owner. Owner-chef Yoshimi Tanigawa (谷河吉巳), born in Hyogo in 1951, started cooking at 15, learned from some fifty teachers in tea, flowers, incense and poetry as well as food, was head chef at an Arashiyama ryotei at 26, and opened Kichisen in 1983; the site lists two Michelin stars in 2010–2013 and three in 2014–2019, and a win on Iron Chef in 1999. Meals are tea-style kaiseki of about thirteen dishes, still cooked by the owner, who goes to market at 4 a.m. Dinner around ¥44,000 plus service; book ahead.

Master Takayama, said by 2026 regulars to know more about Calvados than anyone in Japan, travels to France to source it; there are single casks bottled for the bar and vintages such as a Lauriston 1963. Start with a Jack Rose, then let the master pour a 34-year single cask or a pear-heavy rarity, perhaps with Calvados chocolates from Assemblage Kakimoto. Regulars say it has been hard to get into for a decade, so phone first. Smoking allowed; ¥1,000 charge. Closed Wednesdays and Thursdays.

places.notes: [Bar · Shijo-Kawaramachi, cocktails by the fire in a Kyoto townhouse] Through a small garden off Miyukimachi-dori, a warm wood-lined machiya bar with a long counter, tables, and two rocking chairs in front of a fireplace that is lit each November with the season's first inoko-mochi. Owner-bartender Kenji Tsubokura runs a team whose bartender Kato won a national competition with the cocktail "The Best Scene"; seasonal fruit drinks such as a watermelon salty dog sit beside sharp classics. It is popular: you can book only for 17:00–18:00, otherwise phone half an hour ahead and a seat is held for you. Smoking and cigars allowed, so no minors; ¥880 charge with a snack. Open to 1:00, closed Tuesdays.

places.notes: [Bento · Shinmonzen, Kyoto's benchmark bento since 1829] A caterer of nearly two hundred years, whose boxed bento are, to many reviewers, the best in Japan: some twenty small dishes — duck breast, a perfect dashi omelette, sushi in bamboo leaf, eel, simmered vegetables each seasoned on its own — that still taste right cold. There is no dining room: order by phone by the day before, collect on Shinmonzen-dori (or have it delivered nearby), and eat it the same day, at Minami-za, on the Shinkansen or in your hotel. From ¥3,780; the two-tier boxes feed two or more. Cash only, closed Sundays, and bento mostly pause June–September. In late summer 2026 it also served a limited sit-down lunch of hamo on rice.

places.notes: [Kappo · Gion, the à la carte fish counter] Down a narrow alley off Hanamikoji, a calm counter where you order what your appetite wants from a handwritten board of about seventy dishes. Owner-chef Kouta Endo comes from a family of fishmongers who supply Kyoto's famous restaurants, so the fish is outstanding: Akashi sea bream and striped jack as sashimi, a thick horse mackerel fry still rare in the middle that diners call the best anywhere, drunken Matsuba crab in winter, and a grilled rice ball to finish. Regulars come as a first stop or a late second one; it is open to midnight. Book by phone; closed Sundays.

A June 2026 review adds that the family fish shop is now run by a brother and that simmered dishes are cooked first and seasoned after. Tabelog Award Bronze 2017–2020, 2025, 2026; Japanese cuisine WEST "Tabelog 100" 2025 (Tabelog). · To make the most of the finest ingredients, quickly and deliciously (Waraku 2024). · Horse mackerel fry; sashimi; drunken crab in season.

places.notes: [Kaiseki · Gion, a Sasaki alumnus's generous counter] Yasuo Kida spent 27 years beside Hiroshi Sasaki at Gion Sasaki and was first head chef of its offshoot 楽味 before opening Gion Kida in 2016. Dinner is a long, lavish omakase — crab, fugu, Matsutake, marinated tuna sushi, Kagoshima beef — with portions diners call generous and a pace of three hours or more; each December the room turns into "Izakaya Kida", an à la carte feast of oden and sushi. Regulars praise the chef's warmth. Reservation only and hard to book; around ¥35,000 plus tax and service, more with drink.
